The New Age May Dawn Suddenly

I just put a movie my father made in 1988 up on the Internet for the first time: *Where’s Utopia?* It was the result of years of work, traveling to all kinds of communes and communal experiments around the country, trying to answer a question that for him was primary: How do we live together without recreating the same loneliness, domination, and stupidity we were supposedly escaping?

He had already spent 17 years in the Bruderhof, a Christian community that doesn’t use money internally. They also accepted my dad as a Jewish atheist, making him a remarkably long-running doctrinal exception. In meditation there, he came to his own understanding that “God is the Universe, and the Universe is Love.”

![A painted banner reading “Suddenly it’s gonna dawn on you: The New Age”, with a sun rising over hills, on the wall above a couch in a cozy living room.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!k_WM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Febd8f0ea-e412-4f04-9ec4-d8c000529786_1536x1024.png)

This was the banner my mom painted that hung in our living room for decades. I will try to locate the actual photo.

He might have stayed, but the U.S. antiwar movement during Vietnam needed somebody who knew how to set up printing presses. He eventually founded the Aquarian Research Foundation—not a commune, but a nonprofit devoted to researching how the planet could have a positive future and publishing what it found. His conclusion was simple and enormous: human beings need small tribal communities again, because Civilization Is A Hoax, as I blogged about at the beginning of the Covid plandemic.

That’s where the ***escuelita*** in my title comes in. Escuelita means “little school.” I’m borrowing the word from the Zapatistas in Mexico, whose *Escuelita* brought outsiders into their communities for a while to learn autonomy by living it. In the same way, people would live in the healing communities I’m proposing, to heal and to learn the relational and practical methods, so that some of them could eventually leave and set up another one somewhere else. Otherwise, we’ve built a lovely refuge for whoever got there first.

I spent much of my childhood being carried through Twin Oaks, Acorn, East Wind, Padanaram, Zendik, and many other communities. I was usually just a visitor’s kid, close enough to see how people lived but never quite part of the tribe. At the time, that meant a lot of boredom, with some adventures mixed in, but those years gave me a great sample to compare against.

From 1999 to 2001, my family actually lived with the Love Israel family in Washington while escaping Y2K. In case you aren’t familiar with Y2K, it was the Year 2000 (represented as year 00) computer bug which some folks, like my dad especially, felt might be the end of civilization. We lived in a yurt. At Love Israel, I had my dream of picking all kinds of wild berries in nature come true. I was also lonely, bored, irritated by the cult programming, and missing my friends in Philadelphia.

I wanted to befriend the children there, but they treated me as an outsider. My mom never liked the place. The leader was also named Love Israel, and to me he seemed like the fakest person I’d ever met, complete with the expected God complex.

We spent a lot of time on our knees in the community garden growing food they could sell in town. The money was opaque and seemed to travel mostly upward toward Love. Meanwhile everybody sang, “Here in the garden, there’s nothing left to do-ooo-oo, but eat, sleep, and keep clean!” Again and again. 🌱

My father eventually gave the community his airplane. They sold it instead of using it. He felt tricked, began exposing what was happening, and then we were asked to leave.

The East Wind commune was almost the opposite way. There were maybe eighty people when I was there, enough to have a variety of personalities, small enough to actually make friends. I was happy there. I especially liked showering in a communal shower with both sexes present. I wonder if that still goes on at East Wind? That’s the sort of thing that doesn’t make it into the history books, and which takes some balls (no pun intended), considering how the wider society counts this as potentially damaging to children’s psyches, despite it being the way we’ve lived for thousands of years prior.

Even at East Wind, though, there was some political power usurpation under the surface. They had a nut butter factory that brought in a lot of their income, which seemed to make the woman running it very hard to question. Otherwise, I thought the community had a great social life, a nice way of distributing labor, and no obvious guru.

There were like eight people at Acorn when I was there, and no kids. I couldn’t tell whether it was a commune I might join or a group of people who were already friends, and who happened to live on some really beautiful land and be good at building cool stuff.

Twin Oaks was much bigger, like two or three hundred people at the time, and almost institutional. It was friendly and interesting, but I didn’t feel like I was in a tribe there. It was more like a tiny hippie town, but with a highly structured political system that didn’t seem intuitive for hippies.

Looking back, almost none of these communities had a communal therapy practice. People brought the usual human pain and suffering with them, and it all got translated into politics.

Which meant weekly meetings, run according to Robert’s Rules of Order, with enormous agendas, where most of the things you needed to talk about couldn’t be talked about, and you generally felt like you’d rather be sleeping. (Some people, including me, solved this problem by just going to sleep in the meeting and openly snoring.)

Zendik went in the other direction. They held a brutal community meeting that I’m still recovering from 35 years later. 🤣 Five-year-old me was put in the center and told I was bad because I hadn’t volunteered to help adults with whatever jobs they were doing. Apparently kindergarten had already failed to teach me labor consciousness.

But what I gathered from a bird’s eye view is that the secular communities often thought they could make everyone feel loved and respected by adopting optimal democratic procedures. The spiritual communities went deeper in search of real purpose, belonging, and divine connection, but often put one person in charge of everybody’s inner life. Most of my big little article here is me attempting to describe the missing bridge between those.

Communes Are Hot Again 🔥

Suddenly, the longing to escape loneliness, which inspired my father’s movie, is everywhere again. Back in 2023, ironically, just the year after Covid lockdowns ended, the U.S. Surgeon General even put out an advisory, saying roughly half of American adults experience loneliness, and it treated social connection as a **public-health** issue.

It’s obvious that a lot of people can’t tolerate modern life in isolation anymore (the UN’s rules for prisoners literally ban more than 15 days of it). Folks may disagree about politics, food, God, sex, or whether shoes are oppressive, but they agree that something about the current arrangement is starving them.

What’s starving them is anomie. We evolved to live in small groups where everybody knows everybody. In a large society, the shared norms and close ties that held those groups together fall apart, and nobody knows anybody well enough to see what they’re really like. That’s how large societies end up run by psychopaths. (Yes, I’m always going on about this.)

The Freeloader Problem

Some of the commenters were skeptics tho. The oldest objection showed up immediately, restating the collective action problem: anarcho-communalism sounds great on paper, but when property becomes “owned by everyone, cared for by nobody,” the practicality comes into question.

[![Instagram comments debating whether most people will accept the responsibility required by anarchist communities, and whether communal ownership leads to theft, neglect, and nobody maintaining shared property.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0l9H!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F966a39ab-153b-4d8f-852d-e96421f21f26_714x1228.jpeg "Instagram comments debating whether most people will accept the responsibility required by anarchist communities, and whether communal ownership leads to theft, neglect, and nobody maintaining shared property.")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0l9H!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F966a39ab-153b-4d8f-852d-e96421f21f26_714x1228.jpeg)

I’d say the comment above is more true of the big socialism experiments than small communes, but I still take it seriously, because some people really would rather let somebody else take responsibility. Sometimes you see the same three people who end up doing all the maintenance, while everybody else talks about freedom while lounging around in their hammocks. And then unofficial leaders start gaining power just based on their indispensability.

Any attempt at communal ownership needs to take this into account by having folks take on visible and named stewardship duties, and by having a plan to deal with leeches. The How-To Manual after this essay deals with these issues. No, taking away the idea of a boss does not make everyone less passive, selfish or thieving, or suddenly unlearn their learned helplessness.

Why Communities Keep Dying in the Same Two Ways

Most communes of my acquaintance traded inner freedom of the heart (spirituality) for outer freedom (secular, nondogmatic, political), or the other way around. The two pendulum ends of this trade-off mirror each other. I believe we can combine the best of both, but first, let’s see how each fails individually.

Outer-freedom-only models

The secular communes (and all the manuals I’ve seen on building them) had a solution for how to distribute property or labor in a way folks could agree on, but when the deep waters of jealousy or childhood hurt or humiliation or attraction or resentment or grief came up, the group was without a common method for dealing with it.

Eventually, when people are together long enough, politics will become a way of carrying emotional material that people can’t name. There will be a fight about a schedule or committee or noise or food or some policy or other, but it won’t be about that. There’s no shared way to talk about the hurt itself, but the meeting agenda is the one place the group lets you push for something and win, so the angry communard goes there, trying to get some justice.

Practice group of whom?

Uh, but wait, where do you find people for a practice group? Try an unprogrammed Quaker or Unitarian meeting, a restorative-practice group, any open-hearted congregation, a mature recovery group, a meditation group, or find some people who have gone on long retreats and come back kinder, rather than more impressed with themselves.

And if you can get away from “civilization” for a bit, that can be really valuable to get some perspective on how others have already figured things out. Go visit some real intentional communities. Lots of ecovillages are open to visitors too. Check their current visitor requirements first.

Through visits, you’ll also get a better idea of how much togetherness you enjoy and what kind of privacy you need, and what kind of labor system irritates you. And whether communal showers feel liberating, or make you start looking at studio apartments! 😛 No manifesto is going to tell you any of that.

If you’re lucky, you might find a pre-existing commune that you’d be happy to live in, without starting your own thing.

Practice Before Committing

So, build the part of community you actually can. **Call it a practice group**, for now, not a commune. Do the fun and nice things first, to give people an incentive. Have a weekly meal with two households. Set up a counseling exchange with one friend, in person or by video call. Share tools or childcare. Transport or food prep work too. Or a sauna. And if you’re hippie enough, add acro-yoga, dance improv, a mothers’ circle or a cuddle puddle.

And then the hard stuff comes as a test before any talk of a shared future together. Keep your commitments, or renegotiate when they feel wrong, rather than just avoiding. Get through at least one big disagreement. Dealing with it for real includes the relational pl/ork of each of you naming what really went on, giving each of you time, figuring out what came up for each of you (jealousy, humiliation, fear, old material, whatever), and dealing with it until the emotional pressure changes enough that whatever agreement you come up with means something.

Until all of those phases are passed thru, you’re all still promising strangers, and you don’t want to take out a mortgage together yet. And once you’re past those phases, if you still want to live together, you can all live together in a rented or borrowed space first, long before anyone needs a land surveyor.

From Visitor to Member—Slowly

When The Farm grew fast, a lot of the people who came were in need, and there weren’t many filters being applied. Being open to everybody was part of the spiritual “we are all one” new age philosophy. But practical burden piled up. A membership process is there to protect both the people who are already there and the newcomers.

**First, correspond with the visitor.** Did they read the materials? (Not everyone does.) Do they get the basic idea of why this community is here? Are they at least starting to do the relevant practices? It’s a lot cheaper to find out through a thoughtful exchange than after six months of misunderstanding, right? 2. **The short visit:** If they come for a week or two and just participate in normal life, well, most people can be charming for two weeks. Not exactly a high bar. 😅 So that’s about all you’ll find out. 3. **The long visit:** If you’re not around long enough to actually experience inconvenience and conflict with the person in question, then you’re not going to learn very much about them. Watch how they react when working and making decisions in the group. When tired, corrected, attracted, disappointed, bored, etc. (Hopefully not all at once!) Even a professional faker may be able to pull off an act for months. 4. **Taking on responsibilities:** If someone will have a role in your group that has serious consequences, involving kids, shared resources, medicine, vehicles or private records, you want to know how they handle that specific area of competence. Great skill with kids doesn’t mean they can drive the van down the windy roads safely. You can find out by checking whether you’ve seen them do this thing before, and asking for references if appropriate. Give people access to these things in stages and ensure there’s always some way to appeal decisions about these roles to a separate authority if needed.

Write down your answers: How long is a provisional membership, and what are a provisional member’s rights and responsibilities? How is it reviewed, and how does someone leave it? Who decides on full membership? (Hint: not the person who recruited them! 😜) And what rights does a full member have to the land, the shared resources and a voice in the group, and what do they owe over the long term? (Those go in your founding agreements.)

Then there are the people who aren’t fully “in” the commune politically. Visitors, volunteers, workers, renters and interns at the commune (yes, even interns) are entitled to some rights when decisions really affect their pay or access to common resources. All of them should have clear terms, and the chance to be heard and to have such decisions reviewed. The same is true for decisions really affecting their schedule, safety, housing, records or discipline. Equality that stops at the membership line can end up recreating a servant class that moves from commune to commune.

And when communal therapy processes are pre-reqs for people to get medicine or to be respected members, it can feel like the community is gatekeeping. Well, it is gatekeeping. Some people simply should not be let in the gate, at least not yet. And some people will resent that, and choose to leave, and that’s fine. Some communities will be stricter gatekeepers, and others will be more lax.

It should go without saying that nobody has to take medicine to have equal respect in the community. But medicine is an optional part of the overall therapy process, and if a member is avoiding the therapy process and becoming hard to deal with, they will naturally not belong at a certain point. If it gets to the point of being impossible to live with, they will be kicked out. But nearly always, people who don’t fit in leave way before that.

They should not be demonized for not trying to fit in. They should be offered compassion, but ultimately it’s up to them if they want to fit in and follow the communal processes. And in some cases, the community may make exceptions. If someone is actually sick and needs care, kicking them out could be like a death sentence.

Before making long-term commitments, it really makes sense to go through the choices explained in my below sections about technology, relationships, children, money, and founder power. The exit terms in the “Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution” section after that would also help with thinking about those agreements.

Are Zapatistas just unicorns?

As part of my research I have also looked for evidence of what happened after the Escuelita. While I found information on alumni networks, people bringing practices back with them, and organizing later, I couldn’t find a clear chain of somebody having been to the Escuelita, then a new communal institution being set up, and then evidence about how its members and their children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already spreading abroad before the Escuelita, so if some institution resembles a Zapatista one later, that alone doesn’t prove the Escuelita was responsible.

Sociocracy has a very different history, yet some similar features have emerged there as well: circles, decision-making by consent, distributed authority, and linking between the levels. That means people building institutions of this sort have another serious system to study, instead of inventing their governance during their first dispute.

2. Relational pl/ork

Hearthwork distributes counseling among peers: equal time, attention without interpretation or fixing, and then you switch.

The idea is that the capacity to be there for people when they need help isn’t located in one professional or guru, or the founder of the group that everyone emotionally depends on, but in the community as a whole.

But since we’re merging peer therapy with community, we also need to make sure that the person caring about you and listening to you doesn’t turn what you tell them into administration over your life, the way a professional therapist might diagnose you as this or that and then suddenly you’re ineligible for certain careers. Although obviously that information can come out regardless when people are in close quarters.

Another thing is knowing which problems are beyond what peers can handle and need outside or expert help.

No Special Shamans

Traditional lineages usually disagree with me on this, and many ayahuasca tribes and Bwiti iboga communities believe the medicine should stay under trained lineage authority. I respect what those traditions have preserved, and I’ve learned some “dos & don’t dos” from their sensible practices and less sensible practices. For example, although I do highly value loving kindness meditation, inner child reparenting, and nibbana meditation before ceremony, during, and at all times, I notice a lot of people want their ceremony to look and feel like some kind of abstract mix of indigenous rituals & props to make it feel more authentic and sacred than their everyday life. I understand the benefit of setting aside one time and place for sacred experiences (the book, “God is Red” comes to mind), although the shadow side to that is making the spiritual seem like another world apart from your regular life, which is sort of opposite to integration.

And while I do think it’s valuable to have someone highly experienced in navigating the spirit worlds who is able to sense where you are in those and guide you, I also wouldn’t trust many of these shamans to guide me, considering it’s common to find that even the ones who can heal people very well may still be happy to send evil spirits to kill someone, if that hit job is lucrative. I also don’t trust their medical intuition in general, considering the Huni Kuin shamans are famous for claiming that all other ayahuasca shamans are giving people cancer by using the knotted B. caapi vine (since the knots remind them of tumors). The lineages are right, though, that modern folk do very often decide they’re ready to lead ceremonies long before they’re really trained and prepared. I’m sure I could still learn a lot from those traditions, and they will continue to develop their understandings as well.

My basic issue is with placing one charismatic person above everyone else’s direct experience. The facilitator on the retreat circuit may be wise. Or they may be someone who hasn’t been vetted by anybody, who isn’t accountable to anyone, maybe even a sexual predator, or financially dependent on people coming back to them for more feather-waving. And the more deeply someone is opening up, the more it costs not to personally know who’s running their ceremony.

Even in a culture of peer medicine, there could still be an informal “shaman”, someone everyone trusts and gradually stops questioning, even though nobody gave them the title. I don’t know yet how to avoid this. Things that might help would be to have rotation of roles, and public accountability. The four questions in “Founderism” below apply to these roles too.

Still, I want people to learn to guide themselves and care for each other.

Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection

[![kenyan kids with joel](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Svpw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff76a1545-e84b-406d-8731-1abde6502718_3264x1464.jpeg "kenyan kids with joel")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Svpw!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff76a1545-e84b-406d-8731-1abde6502718_3264x1464.jpeg)

African kids enjoying their childhood! I played with them as my neighbors in Kenya.

My own bias is still toward a system where kids are not solely taken care of by their parents, while still honoring the parent-child bond. If the father is unknown, the whole community can do the fathering, but the biological mom’s role should always be honored, since that attachment is formed already from years of nursing. Kids do need their own territory, places where they can create their own society, invent games and work out ordinary disputes, without always being under the management of adults.

I got a taste of that at a Unitarian youth camp, and it’s still one of the freest memories I have.

The adults still have to pay attention to what goes on in the children’s territory. Older kids can’t be allowed to boss the younger ones around there. And keeping secrets shouldn’t be part of how independence manifests.

I feel very much saddened by the way that adults are seen as (and actually often are) so dangerous for children in the West, especially when an adult and a child are fond of each other. It’s good for kids to have a whole bunch of grownups who know them and enjoy them, who would notice when something changes, and who would act when something’s wrong. When adults panic like that, kids can lose all those grownups without the panic actually preventing abuse. It’s amazing when you travel the world and you see how sick US culture is especially… all over Africa and parts of Asia, I’ve seen parents let their kids run around naked in public with no qualms or concerns. That’s real freedom!

So here’s how I see this protection being ideally structured:

**Give children real agency.** When kids say no to an adult who wants to be alone with them or touch them, that’s a hard line that can’t be crossed. Apart from that, obedience should not be demanded from kids outside of legitimate safety needs. 2. **Create a no-secrets rule.** No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it’s about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. (A surprise has an end date. But secrets meant to isolate a kid aren’t allowed.) 3. **Teach Honesty**. Protecting children is the duty of adults, but it requires children to help also. “The Boy Who Cried Wolf” is a didactic children’s story which continues to be useful generation after generation. The Buddha even taught his son Rahula honesty as the most important first lesson. I agree. We must teach children truthfulness before there’s a crisis. “Make believe” must be labeled as such.\ When adults lie to children (like “Santa is real!” etc), that teaches them to misunderstand the difference between reality and make-believe. Make sure kids understand what they say will be taken seriously if they are known to be honest. Those who are known to lie a lot are especially targeted by abusers who know their accusations won’t be believed. Don’t let the teaching turn into interrogation or punishment when they’re not sure. A scared or confused kid may get mixed up telling what happened and still need protection. 4. **Hear the child even when the accused is someone people love.** Communities fail here, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or everybody’s friend. Decide on the response process ahead of time, before anyone’s face is attached to it. Keep everyone at risk safe first, right away, then make sure the accusation is investigated competently and fairly. 5. **Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community.** Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. State intervention can fail spectacularly, and enclosing kids completely in a community can fail too. Kids need more than one world. In 1984, Vermont authorities raided a religious community in Island Pond and took 112 kids into custody over suspected abuse. A judge turned down the state’s blanket request to hold them, because it couldn’t name any specific case, and the kids went home that same day. There was apparently some physical abuse going on there as a disciplinary practice, but what counts as acceptable physical discipline varies a lot from one society to another, and it happens to some degree in every society, communes included.

Founderism: The Four Questions

In every community there was somebody (or some founding group) who took the initiative to get it started. They found the land, wrote the first documents, taught the method, recruited the first members, or kept things going when everybody else lost interest. Like the U.S. Founding Fathers.

The founder(s) end(s) up with real influence, and pretending they don’t just makes that influence harder to look at. When that power fails to get distributed as the conditions ripen for that, it’s called founderism, which is a fledgling form of what can become a subtle dictatorship.

I’ve seen founderism in many communes that I’ve visited, and I can see it playing out if I were to be a founder as well. I’ve got all these proposals and visions here in my guides, and so it would be very easy for me to become the person who decides whether or not everyone else “understood” them correctly, even while I wish to remain humble and open to the input of all involved.

There are some things we can do to keep founders in check. For one, we can judge the lofty methodology by results people can actually see. Will insiders and outsiders see the members safely flourishing without being trapped? Able to leave without it being stigmatized? Can folks resolve conflicts in healthy ways? Are the kids doing well once they grow up? And if the community is meant to spread, do we see daughter projects actually start up and last? Those questions seem more revealing to me than how big or old the commune gets, or how many decisions are made by some form of consensus.

The questions so far have been about the method. These four are about the founder:

***Can the community respectfully override the founder(s)?*** 2. ***Can the community replace the role of the founder(s)?*** 3. ***Can the community alter the vision of the founder(s)?*** 4. ***Can the community exist without the founder(s)?***

Then follow the practical power. Whose name is on the deed? Who’s in charge of the resources? Who keeps the records? Who decides who gets admitted, and who picks the people who review the founder? Who controls access to the kids, or to medicine, and who can make a complaint go away? The org chart might look flat and horizontal, while the keys, passwords, titles and even just general reputation all point to one person or clique.

If several of these point to one person or clique, they are worth paying attention to before the founder(s) can explain how the situation is uniquely different in a spiritual way. Ask these questions about any community, teacher or method, including me.

While founderism is a problem in every community, it’s especially so in communities which form naturally over time, as I’ve said may happen in my case. In such cases, there’s no formal community and no formal rules until people decide to come together to make them. It doesn’t make sense to do that at first, if, say, I’m the only one there and I don’t know who else will be there that I could trust. If there’s one other person who comes to visit, it also doesn’t make sense, so there’s a critical mass point at which people decide “we were just living together like friends, but now we want to formalize the community.”

If I could find a suitable commune to join, that would basically reverse this problem. I would then be the one on probation. And if we are all starting together from scratch, then we would all be at an equal probationary level with each other.

How My Own Model Could Become a Cult

[![Trust Me, I'm a Scientist!](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!P0dV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa41679e5-fbf3-48a3-b95b-8236dc943f88_1197x1095.jpeg "Trust Me, I'm a Scientist!")](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!P0dV!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa41679e5-fbf3-48a3-b95b-8236dc943f88_1197x1095.jpeg)

I could totally start a cult. Trust me.

As if a founderism-type subtle dictatorship isn’t bad enough, we often find groups that are even proudly and overtly controlled by some Pharaoh at the top of the pyramid, especially when the organization of the group is as advanced as what it took to build the Great Pyramids.

Every practice in this article can be turned against the people using it.

“Nothing suppressed, everything processed” can become a situation where someone in the group must tell all, even if they don’t want to. I have seen that risk in groups that use the ZEGG Forum practice. But privacy also can be resistance to the communal spirit, so there has to be a living, always re-assessed balance between what you and the community owe each other, and what remains your own domain. But some private practices go too far against the communal spirit. If someone starts worshipping Satan, say, they get booted.

Peer counseling can become peer surveillance, even if the tone is warm.

Dissent is important for growth. Sometimes it really is the dissenter’s wounded ego projecting, and that should be acknowledged. But again, balance, because if complaints are too often or too broadly painted as projection, that’s as much a failure, if not more so.

There are some basic human rights that can’t be voted away from you by the majority in a community, unless it’s a question of resource availability as a whole. If safety and the conditions for health can be provided, they should be provided. People should be able to maintain relationships with others outside the community, as long as those relationships don’t interfere with the community as a whole (for example, you can’t bring your boyfriend from outside to live with you if he’s antagonistic towards the commune).

Let’s say a grandmother is demonizing the commune. Cutting off contact with her could make things way worse. When it’s tricky and dangerous for everyone like that, I think the commune needs to step in and help people decide how to communicate with outsiders.
